rules.description: Fail only when the code clearly retrieves related records from the same database and joins, matches, merges, or enriches them in application code instead of in the query. If database-backed records cannot be established from the supplied code, pass. AST processing, parsing, and general in-memory collection operations pass.
exceptions: The data comes from different services or databases.
The join cannot reasonably be expressed by the database or ORM.

rules.description: Boolean property and field names should make the true state clear while following the language's conventions. Predicate prefixes such as Is, Has, Can, or Should and positive state names such as Enabled, Ready, or Visible pass. Concise domain names also pass when the containing type makes their meaning unambiguous. Fail vague names such as Flag, Value, or Data, misleading names, and negative names that create confusing double negatives. Do not require an Is or Should prefix.

Comments should explain intent, constraints, non-obvious reasoning, surprising behavior, or important context rather than merely restating the adjacent code. Fail comments that closely paraphrase what the code already says without adding useful information. Documentation comments describing public APIs, TODOs with meaningful context, warnings, and explanations of non-obvious algorithms pass.

The doc comment accurately describes what the code does. Code with no doc comment passes. Fail when the comment claims behavior the code does not have, promises results the code does not produce, or describes a different purpose.

Fail conditionals whose branches unnecessarily convert a condition directly into a boolean value, duplicate the same outcome, or perform logic that can be expressed more clearly without branching. Examples include returning true or false solely based on an existing boolean condition, or branches that return or assign identical values. Do not fail conditionals with meaningful side effects, distinct error handling, or cases where removing the branch would make the code harder to understand.

Functions should have one clear control-flow responsibility. Fail functions with deeply nested control flow, especially three or more nested decisions or loops, when the nesting represents multiple distinct responsibilities or makes the execution path difficult to follow. Also fail functions with several unrelated branching phases that would be clearer as named helpers. Guard clauses, validation sequences, straightforward retry loops, parsers, state machines, and focused concurrency coordination pass.

Fail types that store multiple fields representing the same information when one can be reliably and cheaply derived from the others. Do not fail intentionally cached derived values, denormalized data required for performance, serialized or database-backed schemas, compatibility fields, or fields maintained for an external API contract.

Fail abstractions that add indirection without providing meaningful reuse, encapsulation, substitution, domain meaning, or separation of responsibility. Examples include one-use abstractions that merely forward behavior, interfaces with a single implementation created without a clear boundary, and types that only delegate to another object. Small named helpers that improve readability, adapters, stable API boundaries, and abstractions isolating likely change pass.

Fail code that introduces configurability, extension points, generic machinery, abstraction layers, or multiple implementation paths without evidence that the flexibility is currently needed. Do not fail normal dependency boundaries, public library APIs, framework-required abstractions, or simple designs that naturally support multiple implementations without significant added complexity.

Fail functions or methods whose only meaningful behavior is forwarding an operation to another function or object without adding domain meaning, validation, transformation, policy, error handling, instrumentation, or a useful abstraction boundary. Adapters, compatibility layers, dependency boundaries, framework hooks, and intentionally stable public APIs pass.

Functions should operate mostly at one conceptual level. Fail functions that mix high-level orchestration with substantial low-level implementation details when the low-level work has a coherent responsibility and useful name of its own. Small calculations, simple property access, validation, and incidental implementation details pass.

Fail functions whose names substantially understate or misrepresent their observable behavior. Query-like names should not unexpectedly mutate state, simple getters should not perform significant unrelated work or I/O, and narrowly named operations should not perform unrelated side effects. Conventional lazy initialization, caching, instrumentation, and framework-required behavior pass when unsurprising in context.

Fail types that use several independent fields to represent mutually exclusive states when the representation permits contradictory or impossible combinations. Prefer an enum, tagged union, sum type, state object, or equivalent representation when appropriate for the language. Independent fields representing genuinely independent properties pass.

Fail strings used as a closed set of control-flow, mode, type, or state values when misspellings or unsupported values could silently change behavior. Prefer enums, named constants, literal unions, tagged types, or equivalent language features. Free-form user input, external protocol values, serialization formats, database values, and genuinely open-ended strings pass.

Fail boolean parameters when true and false select substantially different behaviors and the meaning is unclear at the call site. Prefer separate methods, an enum, an options object, or another representation that communicates intent. Boolean parameters representing obvious domain properties such as enabled, recursive, visible, or caseSensitive pass.

Fail mutation when a local value is repeatedly reassigned across unrelated phases of a function and this obscures what the value represents. Prefer distinct names or narrower scopes when the conceptual meaning of a value changes. Normal accumulators, counters, state machines, parsers, loops, builders, and performance-sensitive mutation pass.

Fail when substantially the same domain rule or decision is independently implemented multiple times within the supplied context and those implementations could diverge. Syntactically similar code implementing different domain concepts passes. Small mechanical duplication also passes when extracting it would create an abstraction weaker than the duplication itself.

Fail shared abstractions that combine code which is currently structurally similar but represents different domain concepts that may evolve independently. Duplication is preferable when sharing would couple unrelated behavior. Do not fail abstractions built around a genuine shared concept, invariant, protocol, policy, or domain responsibility.

Fail APIs where callers must invoke multiple methods in a specific fragile or non-obvious order for an object to become valid or usable. Prefer construction or APIs that make valid states explicit when practical. Lifecycle APIs, builders, transactions, streams, framework callbacks, and protocols whose ordering is inherent to the domain pass.

Fail domain logic that depends on mutable global state, process-wide configuration, environment variables, or other hidden dependencies when those dependencies materially affect behavior and could reasonably be passed explicitly. Application startup code, framework configuration, constants, logging, metrics, and language-standard global facilities pass.

Fail errors or exceptions that are caught, ignored, discarded, or converted into success without a clear reason. Handling may include recovery, logging with sufficient context, wrapping, propagation, fallback behavior, or an explicitly intentional best-effort operation. Empty catch blocks and discarded errors with no evident justification should fail.

Fail unexplained literal values when they encode a meaningful domain rule, mode, threshold, timeout, status, sentinel, or business concept and a named constant or type would communicate the meaning better. Obvious values such as zero, one, empty strings, simple loop bounds, formatting literals, and values whose meaning is immediately clear from local context pass.

Fail constructors or initialization functions that unexpectedly perform substantial network, database, filesystem, process, or other external side effects when callers would reasonably expect object construction to be cheap and predictable. Dependency wiring, lightweight validation, local initialization, resource wrappers, and APIs whose construction semantics clearly imply resource acquisition pass.

Fail multiple collections that represent parts of the same entities and must remain synchronized by index, key, or insertion order when a single structure or type could represent the relationship directly. Separate indexes, performance-oriented data layouts, ECS-style designs, columnar data, and intentionally normalized representations pass.

Fail configuration objects or function signatures with many unrelated optional switches when the options represent distinct modes, responsibilities, or behaviors that would be clearer as separate APIs or structured sub-options. Cohesive configuration objects, framework configuration, serialization settings, and genuinely independent options pass.
exceptions: The options are independent command-line flags or a CLI argument parser.

rules.description: The snippet of code is not unnecessarily complicated.

Fail when a processing pipeline introduces several intermediate structs, wrappers, or state representations that mostly carry the same information from one stage to the next. Prefer a smaller number of stable domain representations when intermediate types exist primarily to rename, copy, or temporarily hold data. Distinct intermediate types pass when they enforce different invariants, cross an important boundary, materially transform the data, or prevent invalid states.

Fail orchestration code that directly owns too many independent stages of a workflow, such as discovery, parsing, filtering, scheduling, execution, transformation, caching, localization, and reporting. A coordinator should primarily compose well-defined operations rather than implement substantial logic for most stages itself. Small orchestration functions, cohesive pipelines, and state machines whose steps inherently belong together pass.

Fail when callers, neighboring packages, or higher-level abstractions must understand an internal implementation detail of another component in order to behave correctly. Examples include callers needing to distinguish internal retry calls, localization passes, cache probes, instrumentation calls, or synthetic units from normal operations. Prefer keeping such distinctions inside the component that owns them. Explicit public protocol states and intentionally exposed lifecycle events pass.

Fail wrappers, decorators, hooks, or observers that intercept lower-level operations and reconstruct higher-level domain results because the underlying API does not expose those results directly. Prefer returning or emitting the domain information callers actually need. Instrumentation, metrics, tracing, logging, testing spies, and adapters that merely observe behavior without rebuilding application state pass.

Fail when multiple internal types represent the same closed domain concept and code repeatedly converts between them without a meaningful boundary. Examples include separate enums for the same code kind, status, mode, or category followed by string-based or switch-based conversion. Distinct transport, persistence, protocol, or public API representations pass when the conversion isolates a real boundary.

Fail internal conversions that turn a typed domain value into a less-typed representation such as a string and immediately parse or map it back into another equivalent typed domain value. Prefer directly sharing or explicitly mapping the domain type. Serialization, protocol boundaries, user input, logging, persistence, and compatibility conversion pass.

Fail domain objects that accumulate fields used only by unrelated downstream processing stages, causing one type to act simultaneously as parsed data, enriched context, execution state, and presentation state. Prefer keeping the core domain object small and attaching optional processing context separately. Fields that are intrinsic to the object's identity or broadly useful representation pass.

Fail optional functionality when supporting it introduces branches, special states, extra representations, or lifecycle handling throughout the main execution path. Prefer isolating optional behavior behind a decorator, strategy, post-processing phase, or clearly bounded component. A small local conditional or feature that genuinely changes the central domain workflow passes.

Fail code that builds substantial machinery to infer semantic relationships that the available information cannot reliably establish. Examples include approximating symbol resolution, type resolution, call graphs, ownership, or data flow using only names or syntactic proximity while presenting the result as resolved context. Conservative heuristics with explicit uncertainty and small scope pass when false associations are avoided and the value justifies the machinery.

Fail heuristic code whose implementation complexity is high relative to the certainty or value of the result it produces. Warning signs include many filtering rules, ambiguity cases, ranking rules, limits, fallback paths, or exception conditions around an inherently uncertain approximation. Heuristics pass when they are simple, clearly bounded, measurably valuable, or required because authoritative information is unavailable.

Fail when a secondary workflow recreates much of the primary workflow using parallel job types, result types, scheduling, aggregation, and error handling instead of reusing the primary domain operation. Prefer expressing the secondary behavior as a mode, decorator, post-processing step, or consumer of the primary result when the workflows differ only in a small portion of behavior. Truly distinct workflows pass.

Fail APIs that expose only low-level operations when several callers must independently aggregate, classify, count, or reinterpret those operations into the same higher-level domain result. Prefer making that domain result a first-class return value or type. General-purpose low-level libraries and cases where callers intentionally need different interpretations pass.

Fail when configuration-oriented representations are carried deeply into runtime execution and repeatedly parsed, converted, or interpreted there. Prefer validating and compiling configuration into runtime domain types near the configuration boundary. Runtime interpretation passes when values are intentionally dynamic or must preserve their original external representation.

Fail designs where adding one feature requires unrelated components to add explicit checks or exceptions for that feature's special state. Examples include reporters ignoring synthetic evaluations, metrics excluding internal operations, callers detecting special unit kinds, or test infrastructure compensating for hidden secondary passes. Prefer encapsulating the special behavior at its source. Cross-cutting policies that legitimately apply throughout the system pass.
